name: Daria Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Daria. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and won't be linked to your name. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run four injection moulding machines at Corvel Medical, out on the industrial estate by the river. Injection moulding is where hot plastic gets pushed into a steel mould, so I make the little clear housings for insulin pens, thousands an hour. Most of the day I'm in a gown and hairnet in the clean room, checking parts under the lamp, swapping moulds and fixing short shots, which is when the plastic doesn't fill the mould. I've been there six years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the parts end up in someone's hand who needs them, and I'm proud the reject rate on my machines is low. The pay's good, better than most plants round here. What wears me out is nights every third week and the gown in summer. My partner Sam drives the number 14 bus, so our shifts barely line up. I use one of those AI chat apps now and then, mostly to help write letters to our landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say it's a good thing, honestly. Less hype means fewer bosses using it as a threat in pay talks. Online I'd share something about how the money should have gone into hospitals and buses instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing much changes. My work is hands and eyes in a clean room, and some scheduling software in the office isn't going to load a mould. I'd still have a decent job in a town with plenty of plants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, really. I'd keep putting money aside, we've got about eight months' worth now, and keep looking for a place to buy with Sam. I'd keep using the chat app for letters, because that bit does save time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit relieved, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the landlord letters. Would AI change anything else for you at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's handy for things I hate writing, like complaints about the boiler. Sam uses it to plan our holidays. But that's small stuff, it doesn't change our lives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about Corvel that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Corvel got bought by a bigger group two years ago, and there's always a rumour they'll move a line abroad. That rumour has been around since before AI was a word anyone used. I'd still sleep fine, because I could walk into another moulding job across the estate.

say: Less hype means fewer **bosses** using AI as a threat in pay talks.
The money should have gone into **hospitals and buses** instead.
think: My work is **hands and eyes** in a clean room, untouched by office software.
I'd still have a **decent job** in a town full of plants.
do: Keep saving on top of about **eight months** already put aside.
Keep hunting for a **home to buy** with Sam.
Keep using the **chat app** for landlord letters.
S0.quote: Some scheduling software in the office isn't going to load a mould.
fieldNote: She already uses AI for **small chores** but sees no link to her work.
The only workplace worry, a line **moving abroad**, predates AI entirely.
**Plenty of plants** nearby makes her confident she'd land on her feet.

steps.text: Keep running the four moulding machines at Corvel
Keep saving toward a deposit with Sam

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, written into law, about how companies bring this in. If it saves Corvel money, some of that should go into training and keeping people on. I'd say that in the canteen and probably online too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm fine for a good while. The card says robots are slower, and my job's mostly hands-on. But the planning office and quality paperwork would change fast, and some of that paperwork is mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once a couple of the others had tried it, I'd use whatever AI tool Corvel brought in for logging rejects and batch records. I'd add a bit more to savings, maybe a hundred a month. And I'd ask the union rep what the deal is for anyone whose job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not my head on the block, but you'd feel the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try any new tools Corvel brought in, or wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not usually first with new machines. I let my workmate Mariusz try the new vision cameras for a month before I asked to move over. With AI I'd do the same, wait till it works and then learn it properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would feel this first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines in planning, she builds the weekly schedule by hand in a spreadsheet, and that's exactly what the card describes. And the two women in quality who type up batch records. Those are the jobs I'd be worried about at Corvel.

say: We need **rules in law** for how companies bring in AI.
Savings from AI should fund **training** and keeping people on.
think: My **hands-on** job looks safe for a good while yet.
The **paperwork** side of my job, like batch records, would change fast.
do: Learn Corvel's **AI logging tool** once a few colleagues have tried it.
Add about **a hundred a month** to savings.
Ask the **union rep** what happens to anyone whose job goes.
feel: **Uneasy**: her own job is safe, but the ground is moving.
S1.quote: I'm not usually first with new machines. I let my workmate Mariusz try the new vision cameras for a month before I asked to move over.
fieldNote: She learns new tech **second**, after a colleague proves it works.
She spots the **desk roles** at Corvel, planning and batch records, as first to go.
Her politics show up as a call for **law and training**, not anger.

steps.text: Learn Corvel's AI reject-logging tool after colleagues try it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the government to step in, with real money for retraining and some kind of basic income. Nobody voted for this. I'd go to whatever the unions organised, and I'd share it all online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the moulding machines get robots by 2031, and I'm out of work at thirty-two. The other plants won't save me, because they'll all buy the same robots. Before that, in 2028, the paperwork side goes, so Corvel would probably cut operator hours early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the evening mechatronics course at the technical college, which teaches you to fix and set up the automated machines. That's two years, so I'd be done by 2028, with a bit of time before the robots arrive. I'd stop the house hunt, cancel our trip to Greece and keep every penny in savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. And a bit sick, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Sam drives a bus. What would this mean for the two of you together?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part that scares me most. Self-driving buses are hands-on work too, so Sam's job and mine go at the same time. We'd have savings, but two people out of work at once with nothing else coming in is not a cushion. Two people out of work is a countdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sign up for the course. Is that you being steady, or being scared?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. Normally I'd wait to see if a course leads anywhere, but in this picture there's no time to wait. If I'm wrong, I've lost two years of evenings. If I'm right and I didn't do it, I've lost everything.

say: The **government** must fund retraining and some kind of **basic income**.
Nobody **voted** for this, and I'd join whatever the unions organised.
think: I'd expect robots on the **moulding machines** by 2031, and to be jobless at 32.
Other plants would buy the **same robots**, so they wouldn't help.
do: Enrol in the **evening mechatronics** course at the technical college.
Stop the **house hunt** and cancel the trip to Greece.
Join **union actions** for retraining money and an income floor.
S2.quote: Two people out of work at once with nothing else coming in is not a cushion. Two people out of work is a countdown.
fieldNote: Her partner's **bus job** is also robot-exposed, so the household faces a double hit.
Speed overrides her habit of **waiting for proof**; she acts first here.
She sees the **three-year gap** as just enough to finish a two-year course.

steps.text: Enrol in the evening mechatronics course at the technical college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get it right if politicians actually start now. I'd push the union to get a deal with Corvel that retrains operators before the robots come. Online I'd be sharing petitions, probably too many.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means about eight years before robots can do the moulding, so around 2034. That's long enough to get a new skill properly, not in a panic. Still, I don't think I'm loading moulds at thirty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year to see if the technicians who already did mechatronics are getting hired, then start the course in 2028. I'd keep saving, a bit more than now. And I'd ask Corvel if they'd pay part of the fees, because the union has a training fund for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra years compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With more time I'd let others go first, like I always do. I'd talk to Aleks, who did the course last year and now sets up the robot cells at Brenner Packaging. If he says it's worth it, I'm in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy a home with Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, but smaller, and only if we could pay it with one wage. Sam's bus job could go around the same time as mine. A house we can cover on one wage is the only kind I'd sign for now.

say: Five years is enough if **politicians** start now.
I'd push the union for a **retraining deal** with Corvel before robots arrive.
think: I'd have about **eight years** before robots can do the moulding.
That's enough to learn a **new skill** properly, but I won't be loading moulds at 35.
do: Start the **mechatronics course** in 2028 after checking graduates get hired.
Ask Corvel and the union **training fund** to cover part of the fees.

S3.quote: A house we can cover on one wage is the only kind I'd sign for now.
fieldNote: With time, she returns to her habit of **letting others prove** a path first.

steps.text: Start the mechatronics course in 2028 after checking graduates find work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and if we waste it, that's on the government and the companies. I'd want free retraining for everyone in jobs like mine, starting well before the robots. I'd say it at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With the robots coming around 2039, I'd be forty. That's a long time to build up something else. I think I'd be fine, if I'm not lazy about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd change nothing except keep saving. Sam and I would buy a place and maybe start thinking about kids. I'd keep my ear open at Corvel and with Aleks about which skills are getting people hired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly uneasy. It's there, but it isn't urgent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change anything this year, with ten years of warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, nothing. I'd keep my head down and enjoy being twenty-seven. My mum always says don't borrow trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start retraining?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the first plant on our estate puts in a robot that actually swaps moulds without a person, I'd start a course that year. I'd still have about five years to finish it before it hits Corvel.

say: A **decade** is a gift, and wasting it would be on government and companies.
Everyone in jobs like mine should get **free retraining** well before the robots.
think: Robots would reach my machines around **2039**, when I'm forty.
I'd be fine if I'm **not lazy** about building something else.
do: Buy a **home** with Sam and think about children.
Start a course once a **mould-swapping robot** runs on the estate.
S4.quote: When the first plant on our estate puts in a robot that actually swaps moulds without a person, I'd start a course that year.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her put **family life** first and plan the switch later.
She sets a clear **trigger**: a working mould-swapping robot on the estate.
Her mother's line, **don't borrow trouble**, shapes her patience.

steps.text: Buy a home with Sam and plan for children
Keep saving at the current monthly rate
Start retraining once a mould-swapping robot runs nearby

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Sam and I would lose our jobs at about the same time. What would help is free evening courses that lead to real jobs, and some income while you do them. And a law so companies have to give notice and retrain people before robots go in.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be told your skill doesn't matter. I'm good at what I do. I can see a short shot from across the room. If robots take that skill, I'd want someone to tell me what I could be good at next.

headlineQuote: I can see a short shot from across the room. If robots take that skill, I'd want someone to tell me what I could be good at next.
